analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act and its companion 2010 law outright, with no replacement.
analysis.headline: The full repeal bill, backed by 5 House Republicans and referred to 8 committees, never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal the Affordable Care Act and the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act of 2010 in their entirety, effective October 1, 2019, and restore the law as it stood before 2010 [S2] [S3]. That would end the health coverage expansions, the protections for people with preexisting conditions, the tax credits that help people buy insurance, and the tax increases that paid for the law [S2] [S3]. It also undoes the 2010 law's changes to federal student loans, which had moved lending from banks back to the government [S2]. The bill contains no replacement for any of it [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the clearest winners would have been high-income households, who would stop paying the ACA's Medicare surtax; medical device makers and brand-name drug makers, whose ACA fees would vanish; private student lenders, who would regain the bank-based federal loan business the 2010 law ended; and insurers, who would be free of coverage requirements — while tens of millions of people would lose coverage or protections [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Repealing the ACA would eliminate the law's taxes on high-income households, including the Medicare surtax on upper earners' wages and investment income, along with the fees it placed on health insurers, drug makers, and medical device makers

Repealing the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act would revive the pre-2010 student loan system, in which private banks issued federal student loans backed by government guarantees, a business the 2010 law had shifted to direct government lending
Insurers would be freed from the ACA's coverage requirements, such as guaranteed issue and medical loss ratio rules, though they would also lose the subsidized customer base the law created

analysis.who_pays: The people who gained from the ACA would bear the cost: those who bought coverage through the marketplaces with the help of tax credits, low-income adults covered by the Medicaid expansion, people with preexisting conditions who rely on guaranteed coverage, young adults on their parents' plans, and Medicare beneficiaries who benefited from lower drug costs — plus the taxpayers and patients who would have again paid the pre-2010 system's costs [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals the ACA with no replacement, ending the coverage expansions, tax credits, and protections for people with preexisting conditions, and restoring the health insurance rules that existed before 2010
It would also roll back the 2010 law's changes to student loans, returning federal lending to banks issuing government-guaranteed loans — a system that cost taxpayers more per loan
The repeal takes effect on a single date, October 1, 2019, with no transition, so everyone relying on ACA coverage or subsidies would lose them at once

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the households and industries the bill's sponsors wanted to help — high earners facing the ACA's surtaxes, device and drug makers facing its fees — the gains are straightforward and real. But the costs fall on far more people: anyone whose coverage, tax credit, or preexisting-condition protection came from the ACA would lose it immediately, with nothing in the bill to replace it. The patient loan and tax benefits for industries are pure wins for them, while the loss of coverage is a large, direct loss for ordinary people. Weighed honestly, the bill's benefits are concentrated and its costs are broad.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to eight House committees and then to subcommittees, where it sat untouched for the entire two-year Congress and never came up for a vote.

narrative.text: Representative Andy Biggs introduced the bill on January 3, 2019, the first day of the new Congress, with three Republican cosponsors
It was referred to eight House committees on the day it was introduced, a sign that no single committee was positioned to move it
Over the following month it was sent to three subcommittees — Health twice and Indigenous Peoples of the United States once — and no committee or subcommittee ever reported it out
No vote ever occurred in the House or Senate, and the bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People who rely on ACA coverage, tax credits, and preexisting-condition protections kept them, because the repeal never advanced. Insurers, drug makers, and device makers also kept the ACA-established market and fee structure they had adjusted to.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People with ACA coverage and protections

for.name: Rep. Andy Biggs
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on the first day of the Congress and gave it its name and framing

against.name: House Democratic majority leadership

against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor during the two years they controlled the chamber

against.name: Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the first-referred committee, with jurisdiction over the ACA
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on January 3, 2019 and never reported it out or scheduled it for consideration

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred; the bill's entire recorded support was 5 House Republicans, and the Democratic majority that controlled the House never moved it.

industries.note: Repeal would free insurers from ACA coverage mandates, guaranteed-issue rules, and profit limits, but would also strip away the individual mandate, tax credits, and Medicaid expansion that supply them with subsidized customers. The bill's death left the ACA market — and its subsidized customer base — in place.

industries.industry: Private student lenders (banks in the federal loan program)
industries.note: Repealing the 2010 law would restore the bank-based federal student loan program, returning to banks a government-guaranteed lending business that had been moved to direct government lending. The gain to lenders comes at taxpayer expense.

industries.industry: Medical device makers and brand-name drug makers
industries.note: The ACA imposed annual fees on these industries to help fund coverage expansion; full repeal would erase those fees. Their tax relief would coincide with millions of people losing coverage.

Repeal would eliminate the ACA's Medicare surtax on upper earners' wages and investment income. This is the largest direct transfer in the bill, and it would be paid for by the loss of coverage expansions and protections.
